title: Glue
blurb: Three seconds, one word, no explanation on offer anywhere. The glue clip travels with a deep-fried pink Doge and has been passed around soundboards, iFunny reposts and Discord servers for years without anyone producing a convincing account of where it began. That anonymity rather suits it. Meme audio of this vintage seldom comes with a birth certificate, and the joke depends entirely on the word arriving with total confidence and zero context. Use it as a non-sequitur, a conversation-ender, or the reply to a question you have decided not to take seriously.
origin: A short meme clip of the word 'glue', circulated with the deep-fried pink Doge image; its original source is undocumented.

title: Homer Drops His Donut D'oh
blurb: A doughnut hits the floor and Homer Simpson supplies the only possible commentary. The grunt was never actually written: scripts said annoyed grunt and left it there, and Dan Castellaneta filled the gap with a noise that eventually made it into the dictionary. Pairing it with lost food is almost too neat for a character whose whole relationship with the world runs through his stomach. Short, and legible to about four generations. Keep it loaded for dropped toast, missed deadlines, and the moment you remember the shopping is still in the car.
origin: Homer Simpson's 'D'oh!' from The Simpsons, paired with a dropped doughnut.

title: I Am God (The Amazing Digital Circus)
blurb: Grandiosity delivered without a flicker of doubt. Inside The Amazing Digital Circus the management genuinely can rewrite the world around you, so a claim like this sits somewhere between a boast and a plain description of the arrangement. Glitch Productions put the pilot on YouTube in late 2023 and watched it become one of the biggest animated debuts the platform has ever handled. Quotable lines were a large part of why. This one gets deployed after minor victories: a solved bug, a won argument, a parking space secured against the odds.
origin: A line from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions, 2023).

title: I Am The Globglogabgalab
blurb: Few characters have ever escaped a forgotten film this thoroughly. The Globglogabgalab is a bloated, book-devouring slug from Strawinsky and the Mysterious House, a 2011 animated feature that essentially nobody saw until a clip of his song surfaced on YouTube in the late 2010s. The voice is oddly gentle. The animation is not. Remixers spent the best part of a year bolting the tune onto anything with a beat, and the word became a password among people who were online at exactly the wrong moment. Somebody in the room will finish the line.
origin: The Globglogabgalab's song from the animated film Strawinsky and the Mysterious House (2011).

title: Light Yagami Laugh (Death Note)
blurb: Death Note is a series about two clever people trying to out-think one another, and this is what winning sounds like when nobody else is in the room. Mamoru Miyano's performance as Light Yagami builds from a private snicker into full operatic collapse, and the 2006 anime lets it run far longer than most shows would dare. Restraint would have ruined it. Anime edits have spent two decades using the laugh as the universal sound of a plan coming together, usually over footage of something extremely petty going right.
origin: Light Yagami's laugh from the Death Note anime (2006).

title: Niffty Laugh (Hazbin Hotel)
blurb: Hazbin Hotel began as a 2019 pilot posted to YouTube, made independently by Vivienne Medrano, before Amazon picked up the series for 2024. Niffty came through the transition intact: one eye, a duster, and a giggle that turns up at consistently inappropriate moments. It is high, rapid and thoroughly delighted. The joke is that she is having the best time available in a room where everybody else has stopped coping. Soundboard users treat it as a reaction to bad ideas, and it works best immediately after somebody's plan visibly collapses.

title: Peppa Pig Intro
blurb: Bouncing strings, then each pig announcing itself with a snort. Peppa Pig started in 2004 as a British preschool cartoon and has since been dubbed into dozens of languages, which is how a small pink cartoon ended up giving American toddlers faint English accents — a phenomenon their parents complained about in print. The theme is short and merciless. Anyone who has raised a child this decade can hum it under duress. It also makes a fine prank on a room of adults, because recognition arrives first and dread follows about a second later.
origin: The opening theme of Peppa Pig (Astley Baker Davies, 2004).

title: Rwarr (Angel Dust)
blurb: Barely a second long, and unmistakably flirtatious. Angel Dust is the most theatrical resident of the Hazbin Hotel, a spider demon with spare arms and no interest whatsoever in reading a room, and this little growl is the noise he makes when something has caught his eye. The fandom clipped it within days. It has become a standard Discord reaction to good character art, good outfits and anything faintly outrageous, largely because it is short enough to spam and camp enough to stay funny on the tenth repeat.
origin: Angel Dust's growl from Hazbin Hotel.

title: So Funny (The Amazing Digital Circus)
blurb: Sarcasm needs no subtitles, and this reading of two very short words carries the whole attitude on its own. Glitch Productions releases The Amazing Digital Circus free on YouTube, which is part of why its dialogue spreads faster than dialogue from shows behind a paywall: everyone has already seen the clip, so everyone gets the reference. Five seconds, flat as a pancake. Reach for it when a joke has been repeated once too often in a group chat, or when somebody explains a thing you understood perfectly well the first time.
origin: A deadpan line from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions).

title: SpongeBob 2000 Years Later
blurb: SpongeBob's French Narrator is a straight parody of Jacques Cousteau's undersea documentaries, accent and reverent pacing included, and he is voiced by Tom Kenny, who also plays SpongeBob himself. His time cards became the show's most quoted running gag. This is the largest leap of the lot. Two thousand years, announced as calmly as one might say the following morning, over a title card that has been screenshotted several million times since. Use it for anything that has taken considerably longer than it had any business taking.
origin: The French Narrator's '2000 Years Later' time card from SpongeBob SquarePants.

title: Squid Game Wake Up Music
blurb: Nothing about this music suggests you are in danger, and that is the trick. Squid Game wakes its players each morning with Haydn's Trumpet Concerto, written in 1796 and about as far from the situation in that dormitory as music can reasonably get. The show uses classical recordings the way a hotel uses soft lighting — to make an appalling operation look orderly. Thirty seconds of relentless brightness. It works surprisingly well as a real alarm tone, and rather cruelly as one for a flatmate who has seen the series.
origin: Haydn's Trumpet Concerto in E-flat major, used as the players' morning wake-up call in Squid Game.

title: Star Platinum Ora Ora Ora
blurb: Stands in JoJo's Bizarre Adventure are fighting spirits only other Stand users can see, and Jotaro Kujo's is a silent purple giant with alarming speed. When Star Platinum unloads a barrage of punches, the shouting is how the manga rendered that sound on the page, and the anime simply kept it. David Production's Stardust Crusaders adaptation landed in 2014 and made the chant inescapable. It scales to any length you like. Fans layer it over fight edits, gaming clips and footage of somebody mashing a button far harder than the game requires.
origin: Star Platinum's rush barrage from JoJo's Bizarre Adventure: Stardust Crusaders (2014).

title: Super Idol
blurb: Millions of people can sing the opening line of this and have no idea what any of it means. The song is 热爱105°C的你, roughly Loving You at 105°C, recorded by the Chinese singer A Si, and it went global in 2021 after a Douyin video of a young man grinning straight into the camera while performing it crossed over to TikTok. The hook opens with the words Super Idol, hence the nickname. Fifteen seconds of unstoppable cheer. It turns up in Roblox videos, gaming montages and any edit that wants sugar poured over it.
origin: The opening hook of the Chinese song 热爱105°C的你 by A Si, viral worldwide from 2021.

title: Thomas The Tank Engine (Loud)
blurb: The Thomas the Tank Engine theme, cranked until the brass distorts. Britain's model-railway children's series began in 1984, adapted from the Reverend W. Awdry's books and narrated at first by Ringo Starr, which is a genuinely strange sentence to have to write down. The internet later worked out that the jaunty little tune turns deranged at volume. Edits use it as a jumpscare — arriving from nowhere, at maximum level, usually at the exact moment a video is pretending to be calm. Thirteen seconds is considerably more than anybody needs.
origin: The Thomas the Tank Engine & Friends theme, used loud as a meme jumpscare.

title: Vecna Clock
blurb: Chimes from a grandfather clock that is not in the room. Stranger Things built its fourth season around Vecna, and the clock is how the show tells you somebody's mind has already been entered: the sound comes first, the visions follow, and the character hearing it has very little time left. Netflix released that season in 2022, and the cue became legible almost immediately. Twenty seconds of slow tolling dread. Good for horror edits, and better still for announcing that a deadline has quietly moved much closer than anyone realised.
origin: Vecna's grandfather clock chime from Stranger Things season 4 (2022).

title: Where's Kinger? (Digital Circus)
blurb: Somebody has wandered off again. Kinger, the enormous chess piece with the frayed nerves, has been inside the digital circus longer than any other resident, and the show plays his unravelling as sad rather than comic, which is why the fandom took to him so quickly. Asking after him is practically routine. Twelve seconds long, so trim to taste. Most people fire it into a voice channel the second a group goes quiet, though it serves equally well as a way of noting that the one person you actually needed has disappeared.
origin: A line about Kinger from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions).
